client: Lately, I’ve been feeling really overwhelmed with sadness whenever I go to my grandma’s favorite coffee shop. It’s like all the memories of her just hit me at once, and I can’t shake the feeling. I’m not sure if talking about it will really help—it just feels like this is how it’s supposed to be after losing someone.
therapist: It sounds like visiting that coffee shop brings up waves of grief that feel both heavy and unavoidable right now. Let me ask—when those memories come flooding in, what thoughts tend to go through your mind in that moment?

client: I just keep thinking about how much I miss her and how unfair it is that she’s gone. Sometimes I also feel guilty, like maybe I didn’t spend enough time with her when she was here. It’s hard to stop those thoughts once they start—they just spiral, and I end up feeling worse.
therapist: The pain of missing her comes through so clearly, and those feelings of guilt sound especially heavy to carry. When the thoughts start to spiral, do you notice whether they tend to focus more on the memories of her, or on the "what ifs" about the past?

client: It's mostly the "what ifs" that really get me—like replaying all the times I could have visited more or said more meaningful things. The happy memories hurt too, but in a different way. I just don't see how I can stop feeling this way when I know I can't ever fix those regrets.
therapist: It sounds like the "what ifs" carry a particular sting—like they're not just sad thoughts, but ones that feel unresolved in your heart. I'm curious—if your grandma could hear those regrets you're holding, what do you think she might say about them?

client: That question makes me tear up a little... She'd probably tell me to stop being so hard on myself. She always said I worried too much about doing everything perfectly. But it's hard to accept that when I still feel like I failed her somehow.
therapist: It sounds like her words—about not being so hard on yourself—still feel tender and meaningful, even though the guilt is still there. What do you think it would take to let those words of hers sink in, even just a little bit, when the "what ifs" start to take over?

client: I don’t know if I can just let her words sink in—it feels like the guilt is stronger than anything else. Even if I try to remind myself of what she’d say, it’s like my brain keeps going back to all the things I didn’t do right. It’s hard to believe I deserve that kind of forgiveness.
therapist: It sounds like the guilt feels so immediate and overpowering that it’s hard to hold onto any other perspective right now—even her words of kindness seem to slip away. What would it feel like to gently remind yourself, in those moments, that grief doesn’t mean you failed her—it means you loved her deeply?

client: That’s a nice thought, but it’s hard to believe grief equals love when all I can focus on is the guilt. It feels like I’m just stuck in this loop of regret, and even trying to remind myself of that feels like I’m avoiding the real problem—that I didn’t do enough. I’m not sure how to shift my focus when the guilt feels so justified.
therapist: It sounds like the guilt feels so deeply rooted and justified that even trying to shift your focus feels like you’re dismissing something important. What would it be like to acknowledge the guilt as part of your grief, without letting it define the whole story? Could there be room for both the love you feel and the regret, without one canceling out the other?

client: I guess I never thought about it that way—like the guilt doesn't have to erase everything else. But it still feels like if I ease up on the guilt, I'm letting myself off the hook too easily. Maybe I'm afraid that if I don't hold onto it, I'll forget how much I wish I'd done differently.
therapist: It sounds like the guilt has been serving a purpose—almost like it's been a way to honor those regrets, and the thought of loosening your grip on it brings up some fear. What do you think your grandma would say about whether holding onto guilt this tightly helps keep her memory alive?

client: She’d probably tell me I’m being silly and that holding onto guilt isn’t how she’d want me to remember her. But it’s hard to let go—it feels like if I stop punishing myself, I’m not honoring how much I care about her. I know it doesn’t make sense, but it’s how it feels.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two deep truths—her words telling you to be gentle with yourself, and this fear that letting go of guilt means letting go of your care for her. I wonder—what would it feel like to honor your love for her by living in a way she’d be proud of, rather than through self-punishment? Could that be its own kind of devotion?

client: That’s a really different way of looking at it—honoring her by living in a way she’d be proud of. It feels a little overwhelming, though, because I’m not sure what that even looks like. Part of me worries I’ll mess it up, just like I feel I did before.
therapist: It makes sense that this new perspective feels overwhelming—shifting from guilt to purpose can feel uncertain, especially when the fear of "messing up" is still so present. What’s one small way you could explore what being proud of yourself—in a way she’d recognize—might look like this week?

client: I guess I could try going to the coffee shop and actually letting myself enjoy the memories instead of just feeling sad. But I’m scared it’ll just make me cry in public, and people will stare. She always loved that place—I used to tell her about my day there. It just feels so hard to think of it as happy now.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a mix of warmth and pain in those memories—like the coffee shop holds so much meaning, but stepping back into it feels both tender and intimidating. What would it be like to let yourself cry there if you needed to, knowing that those tears are part of honoring her and the love you shared?
